seoTitle: UK, Germany or the Netherlands for a PhD: A Practical Comparison
title: UK, Germany or the Netherlands for a PhD: A Practical Comparison
content:
A salaried position, a scholarship and a self-funded place can lead to very different doctoral experiences. Compare the actual contract and funding offer rather than assuming every PhD in a country follows the same model.

Compare the offer, not a national stereotype

The UK, Germany and the Netherlands each have different doctoral routes. Universities within the same country can offer different contracts, funding packages and training structures. Read the vacancy and award terms before deciding what the country's usual model means for you.

In the UK, a studentship commonly combines tuition support and a maintenance stipend. Check whether it covers your fee status and the full expected research period. Admission to a PhD and selection for a studentship may be separate decisions.

In Germany, a doctorate may be supported through university or research-institute employment, a scholarship or external funding. For employment, check the pay agreement, contract percentage and duration. A part-time contract percentage changes the gross payment even if the pay group is the same.

In the Netherlands, many advertised doctoral roles use employment contracts. Scholarship-funded and externally funded candidates also exist. Ask which route applies, which agreement governs an employment offer and whether registration or other costs are covered.

Ask the same questions in all three countries

  • What research question would you work on, and who supervises it?
  • What payment and tuition support are guaranteed in writing?
  • Is the payment a gross salary, a net amount or a stipend?
  • How long does funding last, and what happens if the project runs longer?
  • Are teaching, lab support or other duties part of the role?
  • What would housing and insurance cost in the specific city?

Consider how you want to work

A structured doctoral programme may include courses, rotations and cohort training. An individually arranged project may offer a different degree of flexibility. Neither format automatically provides better supervision. Look at the group's actual practices and ask current researchers about support, expectations and access to facilities.

Language can affect daily life and professional opportunities even when the research is conducted in English. Immigration conditions and options after graduation also depend on your circumstances and the rules in force when you apply.

Use research fit, reliable funding and workable living conditions as your comparison criteria. The suitable choice is the offer that supports the work you want to do and the commitments you need to manage.

Official information

  • EURAXESS research vacancies
  • DAAD doctoral study guidance
  • UK postgraduate research guidance

Compare the same research period

If one offer funds three years and another four, calculate the guaranteed support over each appointment rather than comparing one month alone. Check whether tuition, insurance or research costs are covered separately. For an employment contract, ask about duties, paid leave and recognised experience. For a scholarship, read renewal and outside-work conditions. Also compare what happens if the research takes longer than planned. These questions expose differences that a country-level salary table can hide, particularly when a stipend and an employee salary use different deductions and benefits.
